items.title: [sciencealert.com] Colorado River study finds faster groundwater loss in Upper Basin
items.content_html:
🌾 🔭 ✏️

A study of Colorado River Basin groundwater found that the Upper Basin lost about 4.6 trillion gallons from October 2019 through September 2022, compared with roughly 2.5 trillion gallons in the Lower Basin. The findings challenge the expectation that Upper Basin groundwater would be more resilient because mountain snowmelt replenishes it. The analysis used data from 2004 to 2023. Researchers warn that continued groundwater depletion could reduce flows from aquifers into rivers and worsen surface-water shortages. Virginia Tech hydrologist Susanna Werth said basin water management must account for both groundwater and surface water.

items.title: [leparisien.fr] WMO says powerful El Niño likely to persist through February 2027
items.content_html:
🌾 🔭 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says the strong El Niño developing in the tropical Pacific is expected to peak in December and is nearly certain to persist until February 2027. The climate pattern, which warms the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is forecast to bring above-average temperatures across much of the world and shift rainfall patterns, increasing drought and flood risks in different regions. In Ecuador, the Navy’s Oceanographic and Antarctic Institute reported sea temperatures as much as 5.2°C above normal off Ecuador and Peru. It linked the unusually warm water to exceptional coastal rainfall, rainfall deficits in the Andean highlands and Amazon, and reduced nutrient levels affecting some fisheries. Officials urged preparations for coastal flooding. Separately, Copernicus reported that the global average sea-surface temperature outside polar regions reached a September record of 21.05°C.

items.title: [brecorder.com] Tanker spill reaches UAE beaches, forcing closures and marine assessments
items.content_html: The United Arab Emirates said on Friday, Oct. 23, that oil leaking from a tanker had reached beaches in Umm Al Quwain, prompting coastal closures and cleanup operations. Analysis of satellite images from Oct. 21 showed a slick about 40 kilometres long, covering roughly 190 square kilometres and extending to within six kilometres of shore. Video later showed oil washing onto beaches. Maritime intelligence firms and security sources identified the damaged vessel as the Panama-flagged tanker Gem No.2, which was struck by a projectile on Oct. 9. UAE authorities have not named the ship or said what caused the spill. The spill’s composition and full environmental effects remain uncertain: satellite imagery cannot establish whether it is crude oil or a thin, diluted sheen, and researchers say further assessment is needed. Authorities say containment operations, surveys and environmental assessments are continuing. Beaches will remain closed until technical teams determine safety measures.

items.title: [news.stv.tv] UK approves Jackdaw gas field; decision on larger Rosebank oil project pending
items.content_html: The UK government approved production at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea on Oct. 21, saying it would strengthen energy security and increase domestic gas output by about 6% at peak production. The field could begin supplying homes and businesses by the end of October and operate for up to 11 years. The approval followed a legal reassessment requiring ministers to consider emissions from burning extracted fuel, not just from drilling. Ministers reapproved Jackdaw after a court quashed its earlier consent. The government has yet to say when it will decide on Rosebank, a much larger oil project whose output is expected to be exported and refined abroad.

items.title: [thehindu.com] Pacific waters top 30°C as El Niño tracks toward historic peak
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The central Pacific's Niño 3.4 region passed 30°C for the first time in recorded history on Oct. 5, as scientists report record heat accompanying the developing El Niño, a natural climate pattern that alters rainfall and temperature worldwide. Surface temperatures there reached 30.06°C, and the anomaly rose to 3.48°C on Oct. 18 before easing to 3.34°C this week. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center puts the chance of a strong-to-very-strong event at 83%; the World Meteorological Organization projects a peak anomaly of 3.8°C around December. NASA satellite measurements, drawn from a 35-year record, show the current pattern resembles October 1997, with unusually high sea levels and warm water extending east toward South America.

items.title: [straitstimes.com] Europe’s record heat drives €17bn economic loss and strains cities
items.content_html: Europe’s 2026 heatwaves were linked to an estimated €17 billion loss in European Union gross domestic product from April through September, as well as overloaded hospitals, damaged homes and transport disruptions. Separate peer-reviewed research estimated 50,391 heat-related excess deaths across 854 cities, with about 65% attributed to human-caused warming. The study covered urban areas representing roughly 40% of the population in 30 countries. Britain’s hospitals faced demand comparable to a severe winter virus season, while patients overheated in buildings and heat threatened medical equipment. Wildfires damaged homes, transport systems broke down and cooling equipment failed during the summer heat, according to Bloomberg Economics’ assessment. The European Commission is due to propose its first climate-preparedness law on Tuesday, October 27, encouraging public authorities to consider climate risks in investment decisions. The proposal is not expected to include new funding. The Commission is also preparing a heatwave plan that includes data collection and early-warning systems.

items.title: [insideclimatenews.org] UN climate fund earmarks $20 million in first country allocation
items.content_html: The United Nations’ Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage has earmarked $20 million for Nepal, its first country-specific allocation, after an August flood triggered by an ice-and-rock avalanche. At an extraordinary board meeting on Oct. 22, members invited Nepal to submit a project proposal; the board also set aside $1.6 million for oversight costs. The decision does not release the money, and the fund has set no firm timetable for payment. The allocation is less than 0.5% of Nepal’s estimated $4.71 billion recovery and reconstruction bill. The board is expected to consider its first decisions on other funding requests in December, with up to $350 million available, while 119 countries have submitted 176 requests seeking a combined $2.8 billion. Board members from developed and developing countries also disagreed over whether Nepal’s emergency allocation should influence the fund’s long-term approach.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] GM just did 34,000 years of battery testing in less than a month. Here’s how
items.content_html:
Developing new EV battery technology takes years of research. General Motors, for example, says it’s put a decade of effort into lithium manganese-rich, or LMR, batteries, which aren’t yet in any of their vehicles on the road.

But recently, the automaker says it made a big leap in that work. Using computer modeling, GM was able to virtually test more than 300,000 LMR battery pack configurations, advancing from first concept to formal approval in under a month. 

That represents more than 300 million CPU hours, which would take a typical computer 34,000 years, while running 24 hours a day, to complete, according to GM.

GM is leaning into artificial intelligence and virtual simulations to develop its vehicles. That not only speeds up the time to do testing, per the company, but allows it to test more options, rather than picking the best of just a few configurations. 

Those 300,000 formulations, for example, looked at different chemical combinations, temperature cycling, and other approaches to creating a battery cell, Sterling Anderson, GM’s chief product officer, told Fast Company. 

“If we had not had the luxury of some of these tools, we would have had to sample more sparsely from what was possible,” he says. 

Speeding up vehicle development

GM is bringing this AI approach beyond battery testing and into all areas of its vehicle development, with the aim of slashing the time it takes to develop a car in half. 

Typically, cars are developed within a four- or five-year time frame. That allows a “limited number” of all kinds of tests, Anderson says, from wind tunnel to crash tests. 

“Now in the virtual world, instead of the X crash test that we could have done, or Y prototypes that could go through, we can run X times 100 and Y times 1000,” he says. 

GM is also working to advance its autonomous driving capabilities with real-world and virtual testing. Hundreds of data-collection vehicles are currently driving across the country collecting 1 million miles of data a month, while virtually, GM systems drive more than 3 billion simulated miles a day.

By cutting vehicle development down to about two years, GM also says it can adapt more quickly to external challenges. Many car makers were counting on Biden-era EV tax credits to help their sales, for example, but then the Trump administration cut those credits. 

Tariffs, the war in Iran’s effect on gas prices, changing regulations, and uneasy consumer sentiments have all added uncertainty to automakers’ future product lineups, which may have been in development for years. 

A shorter development cycle “makes you more agile,” Anderson says. 

LMR batteries in the works

GM wants to be the first automaker to deploy LMR batteries, and Anderson says they’re on track to make that happen. 

LMR batteries can have 33% more energy density than lithium iron phosphate chemistry, and use a higher amount of less-expensive minerals (like manganese) rather than more of the most expensive minerals like cobalt and nickel. That allows them to offer more range—potentially more than 400 miles—at a lower cost and lighter weight. 

GM is also preparing to roll out its fourth-generation EV platform, which includes not only LMR batteries but a centralized, upgraded computing system, and new electrical work. 

It will have 30% less wiring than GM’s current EVs and 40% fewer parts in its motors and power electronics, which make it lighter and more efficient. 

GM and LG Energy Solution are working on these batteries as part of a joint venture called Ultium Cells. They plan to start commercial production of the LMR battery cells in the U.S. by 2028, at the Ultium Cells facility in Spring Hill, Tennessee.

items.title: [lemonde.fr] Conservation union warns 96% of shallow-water reefs risk collapse by 2075
items.content_html: The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) classified 96% of the world’s assessed shallow-water coral reef systems as critically endangered, warning that they face an extremely high risk of collapse by 2075. Its first global assessment covered 127 tropical and subtropical reef systems. The risk estimate uses a middle-of-the-road climate pathway projecting 2.7°C of warming by 2100. Based on changes over the past 50 years alone, without future climate projections, 24% of the systems would be classified as critically endangered. The IUCN identified climate-driven heat stress as the most consistent global threat, while overfishing, coastal development, pollution, tourism and storms also damage reefs. The assessment was presented at COP17, the U.N. biodiversity summit in Yerevan. IUCN leaders called for emissions cuts, stronger protection and restoration, and sustained investment in coastal ecosystems and communities.

items.title: [science.org] Study estimates summer heat killed 50,391 in European cities
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Researchers estimate that summer heat caused 50,391 excess deaths across 854 European cities in 2026, the highest toll in their records. They attributed 32,619 deaths to the additional warming caused by human-driven climate change. The study covers urban areas representing about 40% of the population in 30 countries; its authors say the total across Europe was likely higher because it excludes rural areas and a deadly May heatwave. The team from Imperial College London and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine used city-level temperature records and historical links between heat and mortality to model deaths, then compared the observed heat with a climate-modeled scenario without human-caused warming. Heat deaths are often not recorded as such on death certificates, and the estimate is not a count of individually verified deaths. Researchers and public-health specialists have called for warning systems, accessible cooling, urban greening and support for vulnerable residents, alongside reduced fossil-fuel use.

items.title: [ArchDaily] COP31 to Take Place in Antalya, Turkiye, as SP Architects Adapts Former Expo Grounds
items.content_html: The 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) will take place in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20, under a joint governance model where Türkiye hosts the summit and presidency, while Australia leads the formal negotiations. The conference will bring together national delegations, government representatives, scientists, businesses, and civil society to discuss international climate action, including emissions reduction, adaptation to climate impacts, and climate finance. As countries continue to face the challenges of extreme weather, resource consumption, and the transition to lower-carbon economies, this year's programme includes dedicated discussions on zero waste, energy and transport, and resilient cities. In preparation for the event, SP Architects is adapting the former EXPO 2016 grounds in Antalya to accommodate the conference, with plans for the site to remain in use after it concludes.
